comparator.name: Earth, Climate and Technology (formerly Applied Earth Sciences)
comparator.sourceNotes: TU Delft's current programme pages, checked 2026-10-03, identify Earth, Climate and Technology as the redesigned and renamed successor to Applied Earth Sciences. The live programme page states that the formal study guide may still show Applied Earth Sciences while the official name change is processed. The current 2026-2027 curriculum chart, created in August 2026 and labelled September 2026, accounts for the complete 180 EC. The live programme description confirms four integrated learning lines: Principles of the Earth System; Earth System Data; Math, Physics and Chemistry; and Applications, Impact and Skills. Where the live prose uses a slightly different course title, the component name below follows the current 2026-2027 curriculum chart.

components.name: Exploring the Grand Challenges
components.note: The chart presents a combined 4 + 4 EC allocation integrating applications, impact, skills and data foundations.

components.name: Earth and Climate System
components.note: The chart presents a combined 4 + 4 EC allocation across the integrated Earth-system learning lines.

components.name: Mechanics and Thermodynamics
components.note: The chart presents a combined 4 + 4 EC allocation across the integrated physics learning lines.

components.name: Surface, Water and Atmosphere
components.note: The chart presents a combined 5 + 3 EC allocation across Earth-system principles and applications.

components.name: Geodata Fundamentals
components.note: The chart presents a combined 5 + 3 EC allocation across geodata and applications.

components.name: Geology for Engineering
components.note: The current curriculum chart uses this title; the live programme prose describes the corresponding solid-Earth systems and engineering content.

components.name: Minor
components.note: Genuine minor space preserved from the current programme.

components.name: EC&T Elective
components.note: Genuine specialist elective space preserved without inventing a topic.

components.name: Spatiotemporal Data Analysis
components.note: The live programme prose describes the corresponding course as Spatiotemporal Geodata Science.

components.name: Bachelor Thesis Project
components.note: Individual research project with a written thesis and presentation.

alternatives.labelRationale: This pathway gives greater weight to climate processes, signals, quantitative modelling, algorithms, Earth observation, machine learning and image-based spatial evidence.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: This route makes climate sensing and computational spatial analysis the organising priority. Relative to the closest programme it replaces biodiversity, probability, remediation and ecosystem study with linear algebra, algorithms, computer vision and nature-based engineering; the pair differs by four courses and 30 EC in each direction.

alternatives.concept: A subsurface-resource and energy-transition direction connecting soils, aquifers, geothermal energy, carbon storage and critical resources with modelling, signals, life-cycle analysis, remediation, renewable-system design and environmental justice.

alternatives.labelRationale: This pathway centres subsurface science, geodata, numerical and signal analysis, resource recovery, life-cycle impacts, renewable systems and environmental responsibility.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: This route makes subsurface resources and the energy transition the organising priority. Relative to the closest programme it replaces biodiversity, probability, water-management and ecosystem courses with linear algebra, linear systems, life-cycle analysis, nature-based engineering and environmental justice. Relative to the climate-data route it replaces water management, algorithms and computer vision with linear systems, life-cycle analysis, remediation and environmental justice. It differs from each earlier programme by at least four courses and 30 EC in each direction.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest programme covers integrated Earth systems, climate, soils, water, resources, geospatial evidence and research. Climate sensing/geospatial analysis and subsurface resources/energy responsibility form two further independently evidenced, coherent and mechanically feasible directions. All three pass the pairwise 30-EC distinctness floor, so production stops at the maximum.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both integrate physical-science foundations, global sustainability challenges and applied problem framing.
Both develop mathematical methods used to analyse physical systems; TU Delft provides a dedicated calculus course.
Both develop vectors, matrices, linear systems and transformations.
Both develop numerical methods for modelling and simulating complex systems.
Both develop signal and systems analysis, including Fourier-based methods; TU Delft also requires dedicated time-series analysis.
UCR provides selected sustainability-science foundations but no equivalent dedicated mechanics-and-thermodynamics course.
UCR Linear Systems covers signals and transforms but not the comparator’s full electricity, magnetism, fields and waves requirement.
UCR lacks a dedicated fluid-dynamics course spanning subsurface, surface and atmospheric flow.
Both develop geological understanding through applied and field-based work; TU Delft gives greater engineering depth.
Both apply geoscience to hazards and adaptation, while TU Delft’s course is a dedicated integrated field experience.
Both integrate atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and climate through Earth-system evidence and modelling.
Both examine climate drivers, impacts, adaptation and mitigation.
Both apply chemistry to rocks, minerals, waters and environmental processes; TU Delft supplies a dedicated foundation course.
Both study advanced subsurface resources, geothermal energy and storage applications.
Both require applied technical-system design; TU Delft’s project is specific to Earth, Climate and Technology engineering.
UCR studies climate and environmental change but lacks a dedicated atmosphere-and-ocean dynamics course.
Both examine interacting water, surface and climate processes; TU Delft includes more physical atmospheric science.
Both examine how environmental and technical choices interact with governance and society.
Both develop data preparation, visualisation and analysis; TU Delft adds specialised geodetic measurement.
Both develop image and spatial-data analysis relevant to remote sensing.
Both use spatial and temporal geodata to investigate environmental change.
Both use collaborative applied research on a real environmental problem; TU Delft requires a larger international field project.
The genuine 30-EC minor space is preserved without invented content.
The genuine specialist elective is preserved without inventing a topic.
TU Delft requires an individual 15-EC bachelor thesis; UCR’s standardized optional independent-research opportunity is presented alongside it.

notes.text: TU Delft prescribes mechanics, thermodynamics, chemistry, fields and waves, fluid dynamics, atmosphere and ocean dynamics, geological engineering, geodata, international fieldwork, engineering design and a 15-EC thesis. UCR can build substantial Earth-system, climate, soils, water, resources, observation and quantitative pathways, but it does not reproduce that complete engineering-physics and field-project sequence.
